title: 2026-10-06-boreal-systems-reserve-and-burst-fidelity-review
summary: Intro discovery for dedicated capacity with emphasis on isolation guarantees, burst fidelity, and fallbacks. Customer wants predictable p99 latency for chat inference and data residency controls. Security and KMS integration are gating items; they requested a short benchmark and security pack.
action_items: Jordan Lee - Send dedicated pricing + reserved GPU tiers and burst add-on (due: 2026-10-09)
Priya Nair - Share benchmark plan and sample load script; propose test window (due: 2026-10-12)
Sofia Li - Provide list of required compliance artifacts (due: 2026-10-13)
next_steps: Jordan to send pricing and options
Schedule 2-hour benchmark run with Priya and Boreal infra
Security doc pack to be shared by Redwood security by EOD 2026-10-08
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-10-06 14:30 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Alex Ramos (CTO - Boreal), Maya Chen (Lead Infra), Jon Park (PM), Sofia Li (Security)

Summary: Quick discovery focused on commitment sizing and how Redwood Dedicated would handle Boreal's bursty inference traffic while preserving tenant isolation and cryptographic key separation. Lots of questions around KMS, audit trails, and fallback behavior.

00:00 Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick intros. I'm Jordan, AE on the Redwood Dedicated team. Priya is our SE who will cover performance and benchmarks.
00:14 Alex: Hi all, Alex here. We run Boreal's conversational search product. Main reason we're here is capacity predictability and isolation. We're seeing unpredictable spikes when new features ship.
00:28 Maya: Hey, Maya. From infra. We need to understand node-level isolation and whether noisy neighbor could impact p99 latency.
00:35 Jordan: Totally. Priya, do you want to start with how Dedicated is architected?
00:40 Priya: Sure. So Redwood Dedicated offers reserved GPU pools that you can pin to a customer. We do placement to limit co-tenancy, and you can choose physical isolation or tenant-segmented pools. There are warm pool options for prewarm. Sorry, I said prewarm options — sometimes our docs call it warm-pool or hotnode.
00:58 Jon: Can you explain warm pool? Is it like pre-initialised containers?
01:03 Priya: Yeah, think of it as preloaded model weights and warmed KV cache on GPU so first token latency is lower. It's a mix of prewarmed VMs and kept KV cache in memory. It helps reduce cold-start spikes.
01:18 Sofia: For us the big question is KMS and HSM. Keys for customer data must be under our control. Do you support BYOK and dedicated HSM?
01:27 Priya: We support KMS integrations; BYOK where customers manage keys in their KMS is supported for Private deployments. For Redwood Dedicated we can do customer-managed keys via a VPC connector and KMS integration. HSM-backed flows may require enterprise path, we'll follow up with specific diagrams.
01:45 Alex: What's the typical SLO you can hit for chat models? We need p50 sub-40ms and p99 sub-200ms for most prompts at 1-2 token responses but some of our calls are 256 token generations.
02:00 Priya: For shorter completions we can hit p50 around 20-30ms on A100-class nodes with continuous batching tuned, but p99 is dependent on concurrency and batch windows. If you need p99 < 200ms at 256 tokens under 200 QPS, that's feasible with dedicated pools and warm cache. We'll need to baseline with your prompt mix.
02:20 Alex: Okay. We do several hundred concurrent users at peak; typical payloads vary. How do you handle burst above reserved capacity?
02:28 Jordan: Two levers — reserved capacity you pay for, and a burst policy that can spill to either spare capacity in our fleet or fall back to hosted variants. There are policy options: deny, queue, fallback to hosted, or scale up with reserved burst units.
02:45 Maya: If you fallback to hosted, what about data residency? We have EU customers who must keep data inside our VPC.
02:52 Jordan: Good point. Fallback to hosted will route to Redwood Hosted in region, which may be acceptable if you allow that. For strict residency we can configure fallback to only private nodes or a policy that refuses fallback.
03:08 Sofia: Audit logs and traceability matter. We need immutable audit logs for every inference request for compliance. Is that available?
03:15 Priya: Yes, we emit per-request logs with identifiers. For Dedicated we can integrate with your log ingestion via a VPC peering, and retention policies can be tuned. We'll share our audit spec.
03:26 Alex: Cost is a gating item. Do you charge per-token on Dedicated or is it a flat reserved price plus overage?
03:33 Jordan: Dedicated is primarily reserved monthly pricing for the GPU pools plus per-inference compute credits for bursts or overage. We'll include a couple of pricing scenarios — steady, seasonal burst, and heavy spiky — in the deck.
03:46 Jon: Will you give us a sample calculator? We want to model 2x, 4x spikes.
03:50 Jordan: Yep, we'll send a spreadsheet and also a recommended reserve sizing methodology.
04:00 Maya: On the technical side: what about eviction and preemption? If a node gets preempted, what's the failover path?
04:08 Priya: We avoid preemptible instances for Dedicated unless you explicitly choose cheaper preemptible tiers. For failover in the event of node failure we have a live migration/fallback policy that reroutes to spare nodes in the pool and can fallback to hosted. There might be short increased latency during failover.
04:23 Alex: Can we reserve hot nodes that are never shared and never preempted?
04:28 Priya: Yes. That's the isolated tenancy option. Higher cost but no noisy neighbor and stronger eviction guarantees.
04:34 Sofia: For encryption we need in-transit and at-rest specs and key separation per customer. Also API access via SSO/SSO with SAML.
04:44 Jordan: We support SAML SSO, RBAC, and per-team roles in the console. Those are part of our enterprise feature set.
04:52 Jon: Example success criteria for us would be: 1) p99 latency under 200ms for 256-token responses 2) zero data leakage between tenants 3) compliance artifacts for SOC2 and KMS integration. Is that reasonable?
05:06 Alex: Also timeline: pilot in 6 weeks, production in 12.
05:11 Priya: Sounds doable. For the pilot we'd recommend a two-week benchmark: low-traffic baseline, synthetic spike runs, and a warmup phase to populate KV caches. We'll need your prompt corpus and representative QPS patterns.
05:26 Maya: We'll provide traffic patterns and a dataset; how do you instrument the tests?
05:30 Priya: We'll run the Redwood load harness from a controlled runner, capture per-request traces, token-level timing, and you can run side-by-side in a canary with your internal infra.
05:42 Jordan: A couple of risk items we flagged: KMS BYOK path for dedicated needs a security review, and if you require HSM-backed keys on GPU hosts we might need a special private deployment.
05:57 Sofia: Yeah, HSM is a hard requirement for some enterprise customers. We need the options and the rough lead time.
06:05 Priya: We'll capture that and hand it to our Security PM. Expect a short follow-up outlining HSM feasibility and migration steps.
06:13 Alex: From an ops perspective we want to understand warm pool sizing. Say we have 1k concurrent active users and typical concurrency 120 QPS, what's the rule of thumb?
06:23 Priya: Warm pool sizing depends on average request length and model choice. A rough heuristic: reserve enough GPU slots to cover steady-state concurrency plus a buffer for burst multiplier (1.5-2x). For 120 QPS steady, maybe a small reserved fleet sized for 200-240 QPS with burst headroom. We'll work out exact numbers during the benchmark.
06:40 Jon: Do you do per-route routing? Like sending low-latency routes to dedicated and lower cost to hosted?
06:46 Jordan: Yes, Smart Routing lets you route by policy: latency sensitive -> dedicated, low-cost inference -> quantized variants on hosted.
06:54 Maya: Are there any gotchas for deploying multi-tenant models with KV cache? Can tenants leak state?
06:59 Priya: We have strict KV cache scoping per tenant. There was a past minor mislabeling in docs where cache names were ambiguous; we've fixed it. We'll show the cache scoping model in the docs we share.
07:15 Alex: Network egress costs are a consideration. If we fallback to hosted in another region that could blow up our bill.
07:22 Jordan: That's why we encourage region pinning and controlling fallback policies. We'll present a fallback matrix: allow, deny, or route to private fallback.
07:33 Jon: What about model version pinning and rollbacks during incidents?
07:37 Priya: You can pin a model version per route and do staged rollouts with canary and automatic fallback. If a canary fails we can rollback to last known-good model.
07:47 Alex: Great. For benchmarking, we want to test two models: a 7B quantized variant and a 13B non-quantized for quality comparison. Can you run both?
07:56 Priya: Absolutely. We'll recommend different kernel and batching settings for each. For quantized models throughput will be higher but quality tradeoffs may show up; we'll record quality metrics too.
08:08 Maya: Latency measurements—we need p50/p95/p99 breakdown and token-level timing.
08:12 Priya: We'll capture p50/p95/p99 and include tokenization and decode timings.
08:18 Samir: Quick note on routing: default behavior for overflow is to queue for X ms and then fallback. We can tune queue thresholds.
08:29 Alex: Who owns SLA breach incidents? If p99 slides above threshold, what's the escalation path?
08:36 Jordan: Enterprise plan includes an escalation path to our on-call infra engineers and a postmortem cadence. We'll include SLO and SLA options in the pricing doc.
08:47 Sofia: Security review question: Are there penetration test results and SOC 2 Type II report?
08:52 Jordan: Yes, we have SOC 2 Type II. We'll share the report and relevant pen test summaries under an NDA if needed.
09:00 Jon: For the pilot, can you limit the deployment to our VPC?
09:04 Priya: For Private it's straightforward; for Dedicated we support VPC peering to route traffic and KMS integration. If you require full control over the control plane, that's the Private deployment path.
09:17 Alex: Any known limitations with on-prem GPU nodes? We may want a hybrid link.
09:23 Priya: Hybrid is supported but requires extra ops coordination, network setup, and sometimes custom packaging. We'll map that out in the follow-up.
09:30 Maya: Is there a way to simulate production spikes without impacting our users?
09:34 Priya: We'll run synthetic load against a mirror of production endpoints and use a staged canary. That avoids user impact. We'll need a test key and traffic capture windows.
09:44 Jon: What telemetry do you provide in the console? Token-level cost, per-route latency, error rates?
09:49 Jordan: Console exposes token cost, p50/p95/p99 per route, trace sampling, and request-level drilldowns. For Dedicated we can increase trace retention as an addon.
09:59 Alex: On fallback again, could you describe a worst-case scenario where both Dedicated and Hosted are saturated?
10:06 Priya: Worst-case is degraded latency and queued requests. You can set hardened policies to prefer denial over fallback to avoid cross-region leakage. Highest availability comes from overprovisioning or multi-region Dedicated deployments.
10:23 Maya: What's the expected lead time for provisioned Dedicated pools?
10:27 Jordan: Typical lead time is 2-4 weeks for standard configurations, 6-10 weeks for isolated HSM-backed Private deployments, depending on region and GPU availability.
10:38 Sofia: Are you able to provide encryption-in-use assurances or confidential compute?
10:43 Priya: Confidential compute is emerging; we don't yet offer universal TEEs across all GPU types. For high-sensitivity workloads we recommend Private deployment with strict network controls. We'll discuss options with Security.
10:58 Alex: Can you share a runbook for disaster recovery and incident handling?
11:03 Jordan: Yes, we'll include an ops playbook with failover steps, contact points, and runbooks.
11:10 Jon: For pricing we'll need monthly reserved cost, burst unit cost, and warm-pool addon. Include a break-even point for our expected usage.
11:18 Jordan: We'll build a few scenarios in a spreadsheet.
11:24 Maya: A couple of technical nitty-gritty items: GPU memory for batch sizing, kernel selection for kv cache, and prefetch behavior for long context windows.
11:33 Priya: We'll include recommended batch size heuristics per model and kernel selection notes. There's an automatic kernel scheduler in the runtime that chooses optimized kernels based on sequence length distribution.
11:45 Alex: Are there any limits on concurrent model versions? We sometimes run multiple model variants per route.
11:50 Priya: You can run multiple pinned versions, but concurrency management is per pool. If you need strict isolation between versions we recommend separate pools.
11:59 Jon: We'll prepare a short list of routes and traffic distribution for the benchmark.
12:03 Jordan: Perfect. Quick recap: Jordan will send pricing and model of work. Priya will send benchmark plan and test harness. Security will send compliance pack. Boreal will provide prompts, traffic patterns, and timelines.
12:18 Alex: Timeline check: can we target pilot starting the week of 2026-10-26?
12:23 Jordan: Yes, that gives us time to prep. Priya, are you ok with that window?
12:27 Priya: Yep. We'll need the sample data by 2026-10-16 to run tests and iterate.
12:33 Sofia: We'll follow up with an initial list of compliance docs.
12:36 Jordan: Great. Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the deck and next steps.
12:42 Alex: Thanks. Bye.

End of transcript.

Notes: occasional transcription errors - 'K V cache' sometimes appears as separate letters, and 'warm pool' appears in various forms in the audio. There was overlap at 05:30-05:42 where two speakers spoke at once.
